doc.title: Mike Davis interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, April 1, 2024

chapter: Open City and the economics of records
title: Getting it right on the first take
summary: Davis compares film, commercial and big band recording with small-group jazz and his own records, where second or third takes usually win.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Making records: studios, takes and the technology

blocks.x: You’re expected to play the part basically correct the first time. Is that true?

I would say it’s partially true. I mean I think it’s different for different types of things. Like for instance if you’re playing in a large orchestra for a film score, the chances of them taking the first take are very low because there’s microphone issues, there’s maybe some copying issues in the parts, there’s balance issues that they want to go back and check. So you will have an opportunity to get a take or two, and I think, you know certainly in big band recording stuff, all kinds of other, TV commercials which used to be a big thing in New York, typically they don’t take the first take, but you want to certainly be in the ballpark for sure. But I think it’s much different for, especially a small group

type of jazz recording for sure, then you want to be on your game as much as you can be on that first take because that might have a vibe that really lends itself to, you know, the music being served as best as possible and you might get something that you don’t get in subsequent takes. I know in producing my own records, and we just did a new big band record last year. And you know I’m not sure we kept — of the ten tracks there might have been one that was a first take but most of them were second or third takes. But then after that I find it gets to diminishing returns and then you’re kind of like oh wow this wasn’t as good and then now it’s a little bit dangerous when you’re producing it like when do you call it and say okay we can work with this and let’s stay with this one. But that’s what these really good producers have figured out — how to you know, not go over the cliff and start getting diminishing returns.
